item.title: Fed's Beth Hammack and Thomas Barkin favour gradual rate hikes as inflation stays high
item.description: Two officials from the Federal Reserve have supported modest and steady interest rate increases to combat high inflation. They believe these adjustments should minimize disruptions for households, businesses, and financial markets. The Fed has left interest rates unchanged recently, with discussions ongoing about future hikes in December and early next year. The political landscape has shifted following the midterm elections, potentially changing price pressures in the economy.
item.dc:creator: ETMarkets.com
item.content:encoded: Federal Reserve officials Beth Hammack and Thomas Barkin are making the case for a gradual approach to interest rate increases, signalling that policymakers remain focused on bringing inflation under control even as uncertainty over the economic outlook grows, Reuters reported.Their comments on Thursday come as the US central bank faces competing pressures from persistent price increases, geopolitical tensions and heavy investment in artificial intelligence (AI). The remarks also mark the first round of comments from Fed officials after Democrats won control of Congress and made gains in state level elections. For live updates on US Markets, click here I expect that monetary policy will need to move to a restrictive stance to bring inflation back to 2% in a timely manner, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland President Beth Hammack said in a speech ahead of an event in Zurich.According to Reuters, Hammack, a consistent supporter of higher borrowing costs, favours smaller and more frequent adjustments rather than sharp increases. She said this approach would be less disruptive to households, businesses and financial markets. Gradual increases could also prevent an “inflationary mindset” from taking hold, she added.Richmond Fed President Thomas Barkin echoed that view, saying inflation remained “too high” and was holding firm rather than easing. When it comes to the pace of future rate hikes, gradual makes sense, he said.Inflation keeps pressure on the FedThe comments follow the Fed's decision last week to keep its benchmark interest rate in the 3.75%-4.00% range. Hammack, along with Fed Governor Lisa Cook, voted in favour of a rate increase, highlighting the divide among policymakers over how aggressively to tackle inflation.Also Read: Emerging markets lose $33.8 billion in October as investors flee Asian stocksFinancial markets broadly expect another increase in December, although expectations beyond that remain less certain. Reuters reported that futures traders have lowered the probability of a December hike to around 70% from more than 80% on Wednesday.AI investment and elections add to uncertaintyThe political shift could also influence the inflation outlook. Local voter opposition to data centres and permitting challenges could slow AI infrastructure spending, potentially easing demand for equipment and related resources.Evercore ISI analysts told clients on Wednesday that AI capital expenditure could slow in the next year or two, helping keep demand and supply in balance without requiring many more rate increases.TD Securities said it expects the Fed to raise rates by another 50 basis points by early next year. However, the brokerage said a resolution to the Iran war or a slowdown in AI investment could reduce the need for further tightening after March.Meanwhile, Friday's US jobs report is expected to provide another test for policymakers, with economists forecasting 65,000 additional jobs in October after September's 29,000 gain, Reuters reported.(Disclaimer: This article is based on inputs from agencies. These do not represent the views of The Economic Times)

item.title: Emerging markets lose $33.8 billion in October as investors flee Asian stocks
item.description: October witnessed an alarming withdrawal of $33.8 billion by foreign investors from emerging markets, the largest since March. Almost all of this outflow consisted of equities, severely impacting Taiwan. While Emerging Asia grappled with major losses, Latin America encountered minimal setbacks amid election related volatility. Additionally, Chinese stocks continued to see foreign sell offs for the fifth consecutive month.
item.dc:creator: ETMarkets.com
item.content:encoded: Foreign investors pulled a net $33.8 billion out of emerging markets in October, marking the biggest monthly outflow since March, as concerns over technology stocks and country specific risks prompted investors to cut exposure to the asset class, Reuters reported, citing data from the Institute of International Finance (IIF). However, easing US bond yields and a weaker dollar following the US midterm elections could provide some relief to emerging economies.The latest outflow was significantly higher than the revised $19.3 billion withdrawn in September. Emerging markets had attracted $27.4 billion in October last year, according to IIF data cited by Reuters. For live updates on US Markets, click here Equities accounted for almost the entire outflow, with investors withdrawing a net $31.7 billion. Debt markets recorded outflows of $2.1 billion, as fresh investments in bonds outside China partly offset withdrawals from Chinese debt.Taiwan and South Korea bear the brunt of equity selloffEmerging Asia accounted for $28.7 billion of October's total outflows, with Taiwan and South Korea among the worst hit markets as investors booked profits following strong gains earlier in the year.Foreign investors pulled $31.8 billion from Taiwanese stocks, the largest monthly withdrawal in IIF data dating back to 2000. South Korean equities saw outflows of $14.6 billion, Reuters reported. Also Read: Nasdaq tumbles over 3% as tech stocks extend selloff after Democrats sweep midterms; Tesla plunges 9%, chipmakers slideThe selloff came despite upward revisions to earnings estimates for both markets, suggesting investors were reducing sizeable positions after a strong rally. Taiwan's benchmark index had gained 66% in the first nine months of 2026, while South Korea's rose 62%.China also continued to face foreign investor withdrawals, with equities recording $5 billion in outflows for the fifth consecutive month. Chinese debt saw withdrawals of $9.3 billion, its biggest since May, according to the IIF.US midterm results could ease pressureDespite the October selloff, the IIF sees potential support for emerging markets from a softer US dollar and lower Treasury yields. The US midterm election results have strengthened expectations of easing financial conditions, which could reduce borrowing costs and currency pressures for developing economies. The (October) outflows came alongside lower US yields and a broadly stable dollar, which we read as a sign that equity risk appetite and country specific shocks were the main sources of pressure over the month, IIF senior economist Jonathan Fortun wrote in a report.However, concerns around the profitability of artificial intelligence investments and expectations of a Federal Reserve rate hike next month could keep Asian technology stocks under pressure, the IIF said.Emerging market equity outflows have reached $127.4 billion so far in 2026, compared with $18.5 billion a year earlier. Total net inflows into emerging markets stand at $135.9 billion, against $254 billion in 2025, Reuters reported, citing IIF data. (Disclaimer: This article is based on inputs from agencies. These do not represent the views of The Economic Times)
